Across the corpus, the scalability strategies fall into several distinct families. They differ mainly in **what they approximate or eliminate**: redundant computations, the dependence estimator itself, the optimization problem, or the data-system bottleneck.

1. **Optimize the standard greedy mRMR computation.**  
   Fast-mRMR keeps the usual mRMR objective and greedy selection behavior, but caches feature–target relevance scores, accumulates feature–feature redundancy across iterations, and computes only the mutual information between the remaining candidates and the most recently selected feature rather than recomputing all pairs. It also reorganizes data into a column-oriented layout to make feature-wise access efficient. [1377] [1380] [1400] [1414]  
   This is primarily an **exact algorithmic optimization**: it aims to obtain the same selected features as ordinary mRMR while reducing unnecessary work, rather than changing the statistical criterion. [1326] [1350] It is implemented in sequential CPU, GPU/CUDA, and distributed Apache Spark versions, so the same basic method can exploit shared-memory parallelism or cluster-level distribution. [1351] [1411]

2. **Distribute mRMR across machines using MapReduce/Spark.**  
   Another group of papers treats scalability as a data-engineering problem. Fast-mRMR’s Spark version transposes the data into feature-oriented blocks, replicates the class or currently selected feature as needed, computes local histograms in parallel, and aggregates the resulting mutual-information quantities. [1369] [1378] [1392] [1395]  
   The VMR_mRMR work develops a specifically **vertical partitioning** strategy: features are placed in partitions, individual entropies are computed once and broadcast, and incremental relevance/redundancy scores are stored with the feature state across iterations. [499] [507] [522] [564] It further reduces memory and computation by retaining only observed value pairs (“possiblePairs”) instead of full contingency tables or histograms. [515] [537] [546]  
   This differs from fast-mRMR mainly in emphasis: fast-mRMR combines computational shortcuts with CPU/GPU/Spark implementations, whereas VMR_mRMR focuses on a vertical MapReduce design, state preservation, and sparse pair counting. The corpus also distinguishes **horizontal partitioning for tall data** and **vertical partitioning for wide data**. [549] [584] [591]

3. **Approximate the dependence measure with a cheaper nonlinear statistic.**  
   N3LARS replaces mutual information with normalized HSIC (NHSIC), thereby retaining a nonlinear relevance/redundancy criterion without explicitly estimating mutual information. Its objective has a nonnegative Lasso-like form, which can be solved by nonnegative LARS; selecting \(m\) features takes \(m\) iterations rather than requiring repeated regularization-parameter searches. [81] [97] [110]  
   It then addresses sample size with a Nyström approximation to the kernel Gram matrices and addresses dimensionality with MapReduce/Hadoop or Spark parallelism. [103] [121] [135] The result is a nonlinear, globally convex selection formulation, but it is **not an exact acceleration of MI-mRMR**: it changes the dependence measure from MI to HSIC and uses kernel approximations. [84] [105] [115]

4. **Avoid direct high-dimensional MI estimation through a variational lower bound.**  
   VMI takes a different statistical route. Rather than estimate \(I(X_S;Y)\) directly—which becomes difficult when the selected subset is high-dimensional—it maximizes a tractable variational lower bound based on a chosen distribution \(q(X_S\mid Y)\). [186] [197] [221] [246]  
   The bound is made incrementally computable through an autoregressive decomposition, so candidate features can be evaluated by updating quantities from the previous forward-selection step. The paper gives Naive-Bayes and pairwise \(Q\)-distribution versions, both with complexity \(O(NDT)\), comparable to mRMR. [184] [209] [219] [234]  
   Unlike fast-mRMR, this is not mainly a systems optimization; unlike N3LARS, it remains explicitly information-theoretic. Its tradeoff is that scalability comes from modeling assumptions or variational approximations rather than from exact MI computation. [194] [198] [223]

5. **Approximate the global MI-selection problem as a tractable optimization problem.**  
   A separate line of work begins by using conditional-independence assumptions to reduce the MI of a feature subset to a sum of pairwise conditional-MI terms. The resulting subset-selection problem is formulated as a binary quadratic problem, which is still NP-hard. [314] [315] [326]  
   The proposed remedy is not greedy mRMR acceleration but **global optimization by relaxation or low-rank approximation**: spectral and semidefinite relaxations, truncated power iteration (TPower), and low-rank bilinear approximation are used to obtain scalable approximate solutions. [279] [283] [286] [299]  
   Thus, these methods trade exact global optimality for approximate optimization, whereas ordinary mRMR trades global optimality for a fast greedy search. The paper explicitly contrasts the low-order pairwise approximation and global BQP formulation with more computationally efficient iterative selectors. [317] [323]

6. **Replace MI redundancy with fast correlation or dependence surrogates.**  
   Several mRMR variants retain the relevance–redundancy structure but replace MI with cheaper statistics. For continuous data, F-statistics can measure relevance and Pearson correlation can measure redundancy; quotient and difference forms such as FCQ and FCD are used to avoid expensive density estimation. [391] [400] [494]  
   The Uber study further replaces Pearson correlation with RDC for nonlinear redundancy. RDC uses copula transformations, random nonlinear projections, and canonical correlation, with approximately \(O(n\log n)\) cost in sample size. [403] [415] [425] [1318] This makes the method suitable for large data, but it is a **criterion substitution**, not an exact MI computation.  
   At the deployment level, that work uses Scala/Spark, optimized DataFrame/RDD operations, and downsampling before feature selection. [434] [450] [455] This combines a cheaper mRMR-like score with production-system engineering.

7. **Use screening or staged selection to shrink the problem before expensive selection.**  
   N3LARS can be related to maximum-relevance screening: ranking features by NHSIC with the target is a simpler first-stage procedure, while N3LARS adds explicit feature–feature redundancy control. [93] [106] [138]  
   The 2025 sparse-mRMR work similarly uses marginal or dependence screening before applying a penalized mRMR procedure and, in a second stage, knockoff filtering. The screening reduces the number of variables sufficiently to construct knockoffs and makes high-dimensional FDR-controlled selection feasible. [641] [691] [732] [766]  
   This differs from the previous strategies because it does not necessarily make the full selection problem cheap; it first reduces the candidate set and then applies a more expensive or statistically controlled procedure.

**Overall comparison.** The papers therefore scale mRMR/MI selection in four broad ways:

- **Compute the same greedy method more efficiently:** caching, incremental redundancy, columnar storage, GPU, and Spark. [1380] [1351]
- **Distribute the computation:** MapReduce/Spark, with horizontal partitioning favoring tall data and vertical partitioning favoring wide data. [549] [584]
- **Change the statistical approximation:** variational MI bounds, HSIC/NHSIC, RDC, correlation, or F-statistics. [221] [103] [425]
- **Change the optimization problem:** greedy screening, convex sparse formulations, or approximate global BQP solvers. [70] [81] [326] [299]

The central difference is consequently between **exact acceleration** of the original mRMR ranking and **approximate reformulation**. Fast-mRMR and the MapReduce mRMR methods primarily preserve the mRMR criterion, whereas VMI, N3LARS, RDC-based mRMR, and BQP-relaxation methods obtain scalability by changing the estimator, assumptions, or optimization target.
question_answers.global-train-002:
The collection represents the following domains:

- **Bioinformatics and biomedical data.** This includes microarray and gene-expression classification, disease-subtype identification, biomarker discovery, and temporal gene-expression studies. The central challenge is the “large-\(p\), small-\(n\)” setting: datasets may contain thousands of genes but relatively few samples, creating overfitting, noise, and severe computational burdens [814][839]. Many genes are also correlated or redundant, so simply choosing the most individually relevant genes can waste features and provide narrow biological coverage [1155][1179]. For temporal expression data, flattening measurements into an ordinary feature matrix loses time-order information; methods must instead account for changing expression patterns and time misalignment, for example through dynamic time warping [869][885][923].

- **Power-system monitoring and transient-stability assessment.** Here mRMR is used to select system-level features for predicting whether a power system remains stable after a fault, using simulated measurements and potentially post-fault phasor-measurement-unit data [347][359]. The challenges are high-dimensional dynamic behavior, the need for rapid or real-time assessment after disturbances, and the risk that too many inputs cause the “curse of dimensionality,” greater computation, lower accuracy, and overfitting [373][385]. Features must also represent different generators, system states, and post-fault time points while remaining suitable as system size grows [367][373].

- **Solar-energy and renewable-energy forecasting.** The collection applies MRMR to historical global-horizontal-irradiance time-series variables and combines it with an extreme-learning-machine forecaster [983][989]. The domain is difficult because solar radiation is highly variable and affected by cloudiness, location, climate, and forecast horizon; the study therefore considers horizons from 15 minutes to one day and stations in arid, temperate, tropical, and high-albedo climates [1022][1089]. Accurate forecasts are important for grid scheduling, balancing supply and load, avoiding curtailment, and handling rapid renewable-generation ramps [1047][1069][1075]. Feature selection must therefore distinguish useful recent history from redundant time lags while coping with strong short-term persistence and longer-horizon uncertainty [969][979][1000].

- **Online marketing and customer-targeting systems.** Marketing applications include user acquisition, cross-selling, up-selling, churn prediction, and re-engagement [438][448][451]. These systems can have hundreds or thousands of logged user, product, geographic, and usage features, with datasets ranging from roughly 100,000 to 1 million observations [402][454]. The domain-specific problems are redundant behavioral signals, overfitting when all logged variables are used, slow training and prediction, expensive feature-pipeline maintenance, and poor model interpretability [451][462][470]. Production deployment also requires scalable distributed processing, robust computation, and feature selection that works across different downstream models and business use cases [421][434][450].

- **Large-scale and high-dimensional data processing.** Several passages address mRMR as a systems problem rather than a single scientific application. Big-data settings may be large in both the number of instances and the number of features, and conventional mRMR can become computationally impractical because of repeated mutual-information calculations, memory demands, and feature-wise data-access patterns [1336][1393][1394]. The challenge is therefore scalability: GPU, Spark, Hadoop, and MapReduce implementations must avoid redundant computation and adapt to “tall” datasets with many observations versus “wide” datasets with many features [522][549][591].

- **Signal, image, audio, cybersecurity, and other pattern-recognition applications.** The passages mention environmental-sound recognition, multispectral satellite imagery, endoscopic and breast-ultrasound images, pneumonia detection, EEG, human-activity recognition, transformer-fault diagnosis, ransomware or intrusion detection, and handwritten or other image-recognition tasks [1367][1638][1680][1724]. Their shared challenge is that extracted signal or image descriptors can be numerous, noisy, and mutually redundant; selection must preserve discriminative information while reducing the computational cost and improving classifier accuracy [1615][1627][1649]. In cybersecurity specifically, the feature set must capture early attack behavior while filtering runtime noise and irrelevant variables [1636][1664].
question_answers.global-train-003:
Beyond Pearson correlation, the collection repeatedly uses the following notions of redundancy or dependence:

1. **Rank-based dependence**
   - **Spearman’s rank correlation** and **Kendall’s \(\tau\)** are treated as marginal-invariant, nonparametric alternatives to Pearson correlation. They appear in the RDC paper’s comparison table and experiments. [13] [58]
   - The RDC construction itself begins with empirical copula/rank transformations, thereby removing the marginal scales while retaining dependence information. [2] [17] [46]

2. **Mutual information (MI)**
   - MI is the dominant information-theoretic alternative: it measures general statistical dependence rather than only linear association. [305] [271]
   - **mRMR** uses average pairwise feature-feature MI as its redundancy term, while using feature-target MI for relevance. This is the formulation used by Peng, Long, and Ding and by Ding and Peng’s microarray work. [368] [1153] [1188]
   - The same MI-based redundancy is used by the **fast-mRMR** implementation, which preserves the original mRMR criterion while optimizing its computation. [1325] [1359] [1380]
   - It also appears in the **temporal mRMR** literature: ordinary mRMR uses MI or Pearson correlation, whereas the temporal method replaces the pairwise redundancy calculation with DTW-based measures. [921] [947]
   - The solar-forecasting paper uses MI to measure similarity/redundancy among historical variables in its MRMR-ELM procedure. [1103] [1112]
   - The Uber marketing paper uses MI for the standard **MID** and **MIQ** mRMR variants; MID subtracts mean feature-feature MI, while MIQ divides relevance by mean redundancy. [400] [474] [494]
   - The variational-information paper treats subset dependence through mutual information \(I(X_S;Y)\), and its VMI-naive and VMI-pairwise procedures provide alternative approximations to that quantity rather than introducing a new pairwise correlation coefficient. [200] [216] [227]

3. **Conditional mutual information and higher-order information**
   - Several feature-selection methods—**JMI, CMIM, CIFE, SPECCMI**, and related global methods—use conditional MI or low-order decompositions of subset MI to distinguish new information from information already supplied by selected features. [201] [228] [232]
   - The global CMI feature-selection paper explicitly models the selection objective as a binary quadratic problem whose pairwise terms are \(I(X_j;Y\mid X_i)\). [314] [315] [326]
   - The variational feature-selection paper criticizes the usual conditional-independence approximations and instead estimates a variational lower bound on subset MI. [237] [241] [250]

4. **Maximum correlation over nonlinear transformations**
   - The Hirschfeld–Gebelein–Rényi maximum correlation coefficient (HGR) defines dependence as the supremum of Pearson correlation after arbitrary measurable transformations of the two variables. [5] [11]
   - **RDC** is the practical estimator developed from this idea: it applies copula transformations, random nonlinear projections, and then takes the largest canonical correlation between the projected variables. [8] [44] [52]
   - RDC is used in the original RDC feature-selection experiments, where it is compared with dCor, MMD, CMMD, and other nonlinear measures. [4] [10] [18]
   - The Uber mRMR extensions use RDC as the feature-feature redundancy term in **FRQ** and **RFRQ**; these replace Pearson correlation with RDC while retaining an F-statistic or random-forest relevance score. [400] [403] [415] [425] [441] [461]

5. **Canonical correlation after nonlinear or kernel mappings**
   - **CCA** measures the maximum correlation between linear projections of two feature sets. [36] [40]
   - **KCCA** extends this by using nonlinear kernel feature maps; it is listed as a general nonlinear, vector-valued dependence measure in the RDC comparison. [26] [30] [58]
   - RDC can be viewed as a randomized, finite-dimensional approximation in the same broad family: it computes canonical correlation after random nonlinear copula projections, and its relationship to KCCA is discussed explicitly. [24] [33] [35] [1298]

6. **Kernel-based independence and dependence measures**
   - **HSIC** measures dependence through the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm of a kernel cross-covariance operator; with universal kernels it is zero exactly under independence. [81] [87] [612] [689]
   - **NHSIC**, the normalized HSIC, is the dependence/redundancy measure in **N3LARS**. Its objective rewards feature-target NHSIC and penalizes feature-feature NHSIC, so strongly dependent candidate features compete with one another. [67] [81] [84] [95] [111]
   - **HSIC Lasso** uses kernel Gram-matrix inner products for both relevance and redundancy; its quadratic term contains pairwise HSIC between features. [68] [87] [111]
   - The RDC paper compares **HSIC**, copula-HSIC (CHSIC), and **KCCA** as alternative nonlinear dependence measures. [30] [58] [1287]
   - The recent sparse mRMR paper uses either squared projection correlation or normalized HSIC as its association measure, with feature-feature association entering the redundancy penalty. [638] [646] [767]

7. **Distance-based dependence**
   - **Distance covariance/distance correlation** (also called Brownian correlation) detects nonlinear dependence through distances rather than covariance of the raw variables. It is one of the principal alternatives compared in the RDC paper. [6] [30] [58]
   - The sparse mRMR paper notes that distance covariance is included as a special case of HSIC for a suitable kernel, linking the distance-based and kernel-based families. [767]
   - In the RDC feature-selection experiments, dCor is compared directly with RDC, MMD, and CMMD. [10] [18] [27]

8. **Kernel mean-embedding and distributional distances**
   - **MMD** and its conditional/coupled version **CMMD** use kernel mean-embedding discrepancies; the RDC paper treats them as nonlinear dependence measures and notes their quadratic computational cost. [14] [30] [58]
   - They are used as comparison methods in RDC’s multivariate feature-selection experiments. [10] [18] [27]

9. **Information/coarse-grid and regression-transformation measures**
   - **MIC** measures association through a grid-based search over bivariate partitions; **ACE** searches for transformations that maximize correlation or regression fit. Both are compared with RDC, although the RDC paper notes that ACE and MIC are restricted to scalar variables. [26] [30] [58]
   - Thus these papers treat redundancy as nonlinear association in a transformed or partitioned representation rather than as ordinary correlation. [6] [13]

10. **Dynamic-time-warping similarity for temporal features**
    - For multivariate temporal gene-expression data, **TMRMR-C** and **TMRMR-M** replace ordinary feature-feature correlation/MI with DTW-based redundancy. TMRMR-C averages DTW distances over every pair of subject trajectories, whereas TMRMR-M uses only corresponding trajectories. [868] [870] [896] [944]
    - The motivation is that DTW can recognize similar temporal shapes even when they are shifted in time, which ordinary pointwise Euclidean or Manhattan distances may miss. [908] [923]

11. **Multicollinearity and multiple correlation**
    - The **MRmMC** paper defines redundancy as how well a candidate feature can be predicted from the already selected features, using a squared multiple-correlation coefficient obtained through orthogonal projections. [1436] [1440] [1502] [1559]
    - This is more explicitly a multicollinearity measure than a generic dependence measure: it targets linear predictability from the selected feature set, rather than only pairwise correlation. [1516] [1532]
    - The same paper contrasts this with mRMR and MIFS, which use MI-based redundancy penalties. [1451] [1464]

12. **Hybrid or weighted redundancy scores**
    - Some papers combine measures rather than choosing one. The **FCD/FCQ** criteria combine an F-statistic for relevance with Pearson correlation for redundancy; their quotient versions divide by mean correlation. [391] [400] [1221]
    - The Uber paper’s **FRQ/RFRQ** replace that Pearson redundancy with RDC, while **RFCQ/RFRQ** use random-forest feature importance for relevance and either correlation or RDC for redundancy. [403] [441] [453] [461]
    - The improved mRMR paper (**ImRMR**) combines MI and Pearson correlation with tunable weights for feature relevance and redundancy at the feature-subset level. [1633] [1640] [1651] [1695]
    - The improved power-system mRMR paper likewise introduces a weight controlling the trade-off between relevance and MI-based redundancy. [350] [356] [372]

In short, the collection moves from **pairwise association**—rank correlation, MI, distance correlation, HSIC, RDC—to **set-level or conditional notions**—conditional MI, multiple correlation/multicollinearity, and DTW-based temporal similarity. The most recurring families are MI/mRMR, kernel HSIC, HGR/RDC, distance correlation, and specialized temporal or multicollinearity measures.
question_answers.global-train-004:
Across these papers, the standard greedy mRMR procedure is criticized on several related grounds:

### What they see as wrong

- **It is a local, path-dependent search.** Standard mRMR adds one feature at a time, retaining earlier choices; papers therefore describe it as tending to produce a locally rather than globally optimal subset. [104] [156]  
- **It uses only low-order, pairwise approximations to a genuinely multivariate objective.** The exact objective—maximizing mutual information between the whole selected subset and the response—is generally NP-hard, while mRMR approximates it through pairwise relevance and redundancy terms. [200] [216] [232]  
- **Its underlying independence assumptions can be unrealistic or mutually inconsistent.** The variational-information paper argues that many MI methods, including mRMR, implicitly assume conditional independence and class-conditional independence structures that cannot generally hold together. [198] [205] [211] [237]  
- **It can miss synergy and joint contributions.** Because conventional mRMR evaluates the contribution of individual features against the currently selected set, it may fail to capture the contribution of a group of features and can even select an irrelevant feature merely because it is nonredundant with the first selected feature. [1643] [1651] [931]  
- **Its redundancy treatment is incomplete.** One account criticizes mRMR for not incorporating class-conditional redundancy. [1362] [1410] More generally, pairwise redundancy may not adequately represent redundancy with respect to the entire selected subset. [1440] [1559]  
- **Mutual-information estimation is difficult and sometimes inaccurate**, especially with small samples, continuous variables, or high dimensionality. [109] [189] [239]  

### Alternatives proposed

1. **Global optimization rather than greedy forward selection.**  
   QPFS is presented as a convex-relaxed, global alternative to mRMR that solves a quadratic program. [109] [337] Other papers formulate approximate global MI selection as a binary quadratic problem based on conditional mutual information, then use spectral relaxation, semidefinite programming, truncated power (TPower), or low-rank bilinear approximation. [277] [279] [317] [326]

2. **Variational mutual-information selection.**  
   VMI replaces heuristic pairwise MI approximations with a tractable variational lower bound on subset–label mutual information. It factorizes the variational distribution autoregressively and proposes Naive-Bayes and pairwise \(Q\)-distributions, yielding forward procedures—VMI-naive and VMI-pairwise—with an optimality result for tree-structured graphical models. [188] [221] [227] [236] [256]

3. **Convex sparse dependence formulations.**  
   HSIC Lasso and, especially, N3LARS replace MI with kernel dependence. Their objective jointly rewards feature–response dependence and penalizes feature–feature dependence through a nonnegative sparse quadratic formulation. N3LARS solves this with nonnegative LARS, giving a convex/global formulation and a regularization path rather than repeatedly tuning a Lasso parameter. [68] [81] [84] [97] [110] It is designed to scale through Nyström approximations and MapReduce/Spark implementations. [115] [129] [140]

4. **Subset-level mRMR.**  
   ImRMR argues that ordinary mRMR assesses single-feature contributions and insufficiently accounts for joint subset contributions. It therefore forms candidate feature subsets, combines mutual information and Pearson correlation with weighting factors, evaluates subset-level relevance and redundancy, and then applies incremental and sequential-forward search to choose among subsets. [1643] [1651] [1673] [1695]

5. **Different redundancy and relevance measures.**  
   MRmMC replaces MI-based scoring with a relevance measure based on conditional variance/correlation and redundancy based on squared multiple correlation and orthogonal projections; its aim is to measure multicollinearity against the whole selected set without a user-specified redundancy parameter. [1478] [1504] [1563] Temporal mRMR (TMRMR) similarly preserves the relevance–redundancy idea but uses relevance averaged across time points and dynamic-time-warping distances for redundancy, avoiding flattening of temporal data. [878] [890] [941]

6. **Sparse, inferential mRMR.**  
   SmRMR recasts mRMR as a continuous penalized estimation problem, using LASSO, SCAD, or MCP penalties to obtain sparse coefficients; it combines this with knockoff filtering to control the false-discovery rate instead of requiring a fixed number of selected features. [633] [657] [678] [777]

In short, the common diagnosis is that greedy mRMR is **pairwise, assumption-heavy, locally optimized, and weak at representing group effects**. The proposed responses are to optimize subsets globally, model mutual information variationally, use convex sparse dependence objectives, evaluate feature groups directly, replace pairwise redundancy with multivariate or domain-specific measures, or add statistical sparsity and error control.
question_answers.global-train-005:
The collection shows several recurring pairings:

- **mRMR + a classifier/wrapper, especially SVM.** The filter first generates a ranked or nested set of candidate subsets; an SVM then evaluates their classification accuracy and chooses the best subset. This combines mRMR’s relevance–redundancy screening with classifier-specific validation, avoiding exhaustive search while selecting the subset that performs best for the task. [352] [356] [381]

- **mRMR + Extreme Learning Machine (ELM).** In solar-irradiance forecasting, mRMR selects relevant, minimally redundant historical variables, and ELM uses them for forecasting. The purpose is to reduce the input dimensionality and noise while retaining variables that improve forecasting performance; the ELM is also attractive for its fast training. [989] [1009] [1035] [1049]

- **mRMR + Boruta/Random Forest.** The BoMGene pipeline uses mRMR for the initial global reduction, then Boruta—with randomized shadow features and Random Forest importance—to refine the reduced set. The rationale is that mRMR is fast, model-agnostic, and removes much redundancy, whereas Boruta performs a more model-aware test for truly influential variables; applying Boruta after screening also reduces its computational burden and overfitting risk. [789] [823] [829] [836] [838]

- **mRMR + ReliefF.** One described two-stage mRMR–ReliefF design uses ReliefF to identify informative candidate genes and mRMR afterward to remove redundancy and form the final subset. The intended benefit is to combine ReliefF’s ability to find informative features with mRMR’s control of inter-feature redundancy. [798]

- **mRMR + metaheuristic search/optimization.** The collection mentions combinations with the **Bat algorithm**, which searches the mRMR-prefiltered genes for an optimal subset; with **genetic algorithms**, which search for an optimal or near-optimal subset after information-based filtering; with **particle-swarm optimization**, which uses mRMR inside the search process; and with **simulated annealing plus Rao optimization**, which improves the solution after mRMR selects relevant genes. These techniques are used because mRMR is a greedy filter, while global or heuristic search can further optimize the subset and improve classification or search efficiency. [850] [1599] [1713] [1704]

- **mRMR-style filtering + sequential forward selection (SFS/SFSFs).** The improved ImRMR method ranks features and candidate subsets using Pearson correlation and mutual information, then applies incremental search and sequence-forward search to obtain the final subset. The second stage is intended to account for the joint contribution of multiple features rather than relying only on individual-feature scores, and to select the subset that achieves the desired classification performance. [1602] [1619] [1633] [1650]

- **mRMR-style filtering + DTW for temporal data.** TMRMR retains the mRMR relevance–redundancy framework but replaces ordinary redundancy calculations with dynamic time warping (DTW), while relevance is aggregated across time points. This is done to preserve temporal information without flattening multivariate time series and to recognize similarity between expression trajectories that may be shifted in time. [878] [890] [923] [947]

- **Sparse mRMR + the knockoff filter.** The newer SmRMR pipeline first screens variables with a penalized mRMR criterion and then applies model-X knockoffs to control the false discovery rate. The first stage reduces the ultra-high-dimensional search space; the knockoff stage provides statistically controlled selection rather than merely choosing a fixed number of features. [622] [631] [652] [766]

Overall, the pairings serve two main purposes: **mRMR provides fast, model-independent relevance and redundancy reduction**, while the second technique either **optimizes or validates the subset for a particular predictive task**, **captures nonlinear/temporal structure**, or **adds statistical error control**. [133] [149] [1555]
question_answers.global-train-006:
The collection divides into two broad camps:

### 1. Papers that model an explicit temporal dimension

These papers do not treat every time point simply as an unrelated static column; they retain or exploit temporal structure.

- **Radovic et al., “Minimum redundancy maximum relevance feature selection approach for temporal gene expression data.”** This is the clearest temporal case. The paper explicitly argues that ordinary feature-selection methods require flattening multivariate temporal data, which loses temporal information, and proposes TMRMR to avoid that flattening [869]. Relevance is aggregated across time points, while redundancy is computed using dynamic time warping (DTW) between gene-expression trajectories [885] [947]. Its two variants are **TMRMR-C** and **TMRMR-M** [896].
- **Bouzgou and Gueymard, “Minimum redundancy – Maximum relevance with extreme learning machines for global solar radiation forecasting.”** This paper treats historical observations as time-series variables for forecasting, selecting a subset of past values before using an ELM predictor [983] [998]. It compares a long window, short window, PCA, and MRMR-based selection of historical variables [1007] [1013].
- **Li and Gu, “Feature Selection for Transient Stability Assessment Based on Improved Maximal Relevance and Minimal Redundancy Criterion.”** This is a borderline temporal case: the method is still a tabular feature-selection pipeline, but its feature set explicitly contains measurements at multiple stages after a fault, and the paper distinguishes static from dynamic features [373]. The temporal process is represented through timestamped features such as measurements at fault-clearing time and several subsequent cycles [349] [358], rather than through a sequence model or a trajectory-distance method.

### 2. Papers treating data as ordinary static tabular samples

Most of the collection belongs here. These works represent each observation as a row and each feature as a column, applying dependence, mutual-information, kernel, or feature-selection criteria without modeling an intrinsic time axis.

- **Lopez-Paz, Hennig, and Schölkopf, “The Randomized Dependence Coefficient.”** RDC is defined for paired random samples \(X\) and \(Y\), including multidimensional vectors, and its experiments use heterogeneous UCI and other tabular datasets [25] [1287]. It does not introduce a temporal index; it operates on empirical copula transformations and random nonlinear projections [46] [52].
- **Yamada et al., “N3LARS: Minimum Redundancy Maximum Relevance Feature Selection for Large and High-dimensional Data.”** The formulation assumes i.i.d. paired samples and a dense feature vector [128] [136]. Its experiments use ordinary classification and regression tables, including UCI, image, gene-expression, and other high-dimensional datasets [78] [101].
- **Gao, Ver Steeg, and Galstyan, “Variational Information Maximization for Feature Selection.”** This paper formulates the input as a \(D\)-dimensional feature vector and evaluates feature selection on conventional labeled datasets [189] [200] [214]. The “step” notation refers to the sequential selection algorithm, not an observed temporal axis [216].

The collection shows several recurring ways to collapse relevance and redundancy into a single criterion:

1. **Difference / additive penalty.**  
   The standard mRMR-style rule subtracts average redundancy from relevance:
   \[
   \text{score}=\text{relevance}-\text{redundancy}.
   \]
   This appears as MID for mutual information and FCD for an F-statistic combined with correlation. It is simple and computationally convenient, but it implicitly treats the two terms as directly comparable and equally weighted. [400] [391] [1213]  
   A key weakness is **scale mismatch**: an F-statistic can take arbitrarily large positive values, whereas correlation lies between zero and one, so relevance may dominate and make redundancy ineffective. [1471] [1508]

2. **Quotient / divisive combination.**  
   MIQ and FCQ divide relevance by redundancy rather than subtracting it:
   \[
   \text{score}=\frac{\text{relevance}}{\text{redundancy}}.
   \]
   The same pattern is used with other relevance–redundancy pairs, such as F-statistic/RDC quotients and random-forest-importance quotients. [400] [494] [403] [441]  
   The claimed advantage is greater robustness to differences in scale between the two measures. [445] [453] In the original mRMR experiments, the quotient was reported to impose a stronger penalty on redundant features and was generally preferred: MIQ performed better for discrete data, FCQ for continuous data, and the quotient-selected sets had lower redundancy. [1156] [1160] [1177] [1181]  
   The tradeoff is that quotient methods can favor a feature with modest relevance if its redundancy is exceptionally small; the passages identify the stronger redundancy penalty, but do not establish that this behavior is always desirable.

3. **Weighted difference.**  
   An explicit weight can interpolate between relevance and redundancy:
   \[
   \text{score}=\alpha\,\text{relevance}-(1-\alpha)\,\text{redundancy}.
   \]
   With \(\alpha=0.5\), this reduces to ordinary mRMR; varying \(\alpha\) changes the feature ordering and lets the practitioner control how much redundancy matters. [372]  
   The reported benefit is finer control: in one application, changing the weight improved the best classification accuracy from 97.5% to 99% while reducing the selected subset from ten to seven features. [370] The cost is an additional tuning choice, since different weights produce different rankings and subsets. [351] [357]

4. **Joint optimization rather than a fixed scalar score.**  
   Some methods embed relevance and redundancy in an optimization objective instead of only ranking candidates by a scalar difference or quotient. HSIC Lasso/N3LARS, for example, has a linear relevance term and a quadratic feature–feature redundancy term; strong feature–feature dependence tends to drive one of the competing coefficients toward zero. [81] [87] [111]  
   This can model redundancy among the selected features more jointly and can yield non-redundant sparse sets, but it introduces optimization, regularization, and computational costs; HSIC Lasso, for example, requires substantial memory and tuning of its regularization parameter. [111] [129] [110]

Overall, the central tradeoff is between **simplicity and tunability**: subtraction is transparent but sensitive to scale and weighting; quotients reduce scale sensitivity and often penalize redundancy more aggressively; weighted or optimization-based formulations offer finer control or richer joint modeling, but require parameter selection and/or more computation. [1471] [1508] [445] [110]

Across the papers, feature selection is repeatedly motivated by a common set of goals:

- **Reduce dimensionality and computational burden.** Selecting a smaller subset makes training and prediction faster, reduces memory and resource use, and enables methods to operate on high-dimensional or large-scale data [287][402][470][578]. Several papers specifically frame scalability as a central problem when the number of features or samples is very large [1336][1393][1401].

- **Improve predictive performance and generalization.** Irrelevant or noisy variables can hurt accuracy, increase model complexity, and lead to overfitting; removing them is therefore expected to improve robustness on unseen data [213][287][418][819]. The papers also stress that adding more features does not necessarily improve performance and can eventually make it worse [290][361].

- **Remove redundancy while retaining complementary information.** A recurring distinction is between merely choosing relevant variables and choosing a subset that is also non-redundant. Highly correlated features may contribute little new information, waste part of the feature budget, and fail to represent the target broadly [75][1155][1179]. Hence the widespread “maximum relevance–minimum redundancy” motivation: retain features related to the target but avoid selecting near-duplicates [397][737].

- **Produce a more informative and representative compact subset.** The aim is not simply fewer variables, but a subset that preserves the useful structure or predictive information in the original data while covering it more broadly [1166][1191][1231]. This can allow a smaller subset to match or outperform a much larger conventional feature set [1214].

- **Improve interpretability and scientific or operational insight.** Keeping original variables, rather than replacing them with opaque combinations, makes it easier to understand what drives predictions and to identify meaningful biomarkers or system variables [1328][1506]. This motivation appears in applications ranging from gene selection and disease analysis [1161][1172] to production marketing systems, where fewer features make model diagnosis and compliance easier [483].

- **Make the resulting model simpler and more deployable.** Smaller inputs support simpler models, easier maintenance, faster deployment, and lower data-pipeline monitoring costs [402][470][488]. In some applications, selection is explicitly treated as a necessary preprocessing step before model construction [509][570].

In short, the recurring rationale is: **discard irrelevant, noisy, and redundant information so that learning is faster, less prone to overfitting, more accurate or robust, easier to interpret, and feasible at scale** [207][213][287][402].

Both papers recognize that greedy mutual-information (MI) selection becomes tractable only by imposing strong independence assumptions, but they respond differently:

- **Gao, Ver Steeg & Galstyan reject the usual pair of assumptions as a general foundation.** They show that common MI approximations factor high-dimensional conditional entropies into sums of pairwise terms, which is exact only if both ordinary conditional independence and class-conditional independence hold [237]. They argue these assumptions are generally mutually inconsistent: conditioning on a candidate feature may make selected features independent, but conditioning on that feature and the class label usually leaves dependencies mediated by the class [205][211]. Their remedy is **variational**: replace direct high-dimensional MI estimation with a tractable lower bound based on a chosen variational distribution [246][250]. They use autoregressive distributions, including Naive Bayes and pairwise forms, so the method can still select features forward without asserting that the data truly satisfy the traditional independence assumptions [227][184]. Importantly, they prove that even the Naive-Bayes variational method is optimal for data generated by tree graphical models, rather than only for a Naive-Bayes model [236][191].

- **Venkateswara et al. accept the conditional-independence assumption as an approximation and change the optimization problem.** They explicitly assume that, given a candidate feature \(X_i\), the already selected features are both marginally and class-conditionally independent [298][308]. Under this assumption, the MI of a subset is approximated by the candidate’s relevance \(I(X_i;Y)\) plus pairwise conditional-MI terms \(I(X_j;Y\mid X_i)\) [315][319]. The resulting subset-selection objective is formulated as a **binary quadratic problem (BQP)**, which is NP-hard, and they use linear, spectral, semidefinite, truncated-power, and low-rank relaxations to obtain approximate global solutions [326][267][317]. Thus, their response is not to remove the independence assumption, but to use it to move beyond greedy selection toward a global, combinatorial optimization problem.

**In short:** Gao et al. treat the standard independence assumptions as theoretically problematic and replace them with flexible variational approximations that can yield guarantees under structured models [241][188]. Venkateswara et al. retain the assumption, use it to reduce high-order MI to pairwise CMI, and then address the remaining difficulty—global subset selection—through BQP approximations [314][326].

The bottlenecks are at different levels:

- **RDC addresses the cost of constructing a practical dependence measure.** The underlying HGR maximum-correlation definition is intractable because it optimizes over an infinite-dimensional function space [25]. Existing nonlinear measures such as KCCA, HSIC, dCor, and MIC can also have at least quadratic cost in the number of samples [30]. RDC replaces that expensive/general optimization with finite random nonlinear copula projections and canonical correlation, achieving approximately \(O(n\log n)\) cost in sample size [44][48][57]. Thus, RDC’s bottleneck is primarily **measuring dependence between variables efficiently**, especially as the number of observations grows.

- **Fast-mRMR addresses the cost of repeatedly using dependence scores during feature selection.** Standard mRMR’s main bottleneck is computing mutual information between feature–class pairs and feature–feature pairs [1359][1363]. Its cost scales quadratically with the number of features and linearly with the number of samples [1362]. Fast-mRMR therefore reduces repeated and unnecessary computations: it accumulates redundancy so that each iteration only computes MI with the newly selected feature, caches relevance and marginal quantities, and uses improved data-access patterns [1380][1381]. Its bottleneck is consequently **the feature-selection procedure’s repeated, high-dimensional use of pairwise dependence calculations**, not the fundamental construction of a new dependence statistic.

In short: **RDC makes nonlinear dependence measurement itself scalable in \(n\); Fast-mRMR makes greedy mRMR selection scalable in the number of features by avoiding redundant MI computations.** Both reduce dependence-related cost, but RDC targets the *dependence estimator*, whereas Fast-mRMR targets the *algorithmic workload generated by repeatedly applying dependence estimates*.

The papers assign mutual information (MI) three distinct roles:

1. **MI as a direct selection criterion.**  
   In the variational-information feature-selection paper, the ideal filter objective is stated directly: choose a subset \(S\) of fixed size that maximizes \(I(x_S:y)\), the mutual information between the selected features and the class label [200]. Greedy versions then add the feature that produces the largest increase in this MI objective [216]. Thus, MI is not merely descriptive; it is the quantity being optimized to define the “best” feature subset.

   The mRMR paper uses MI more operationally: it measures each feature’s relevance to the class and the redundancy between selected features, then combines the two into a difference or quotient criterion [1166] [1171]. Here MI directly determines the feature ranking, although the full multivariate objective is handled through a greedy approximation.

2. **MI as a target to be approximated.**  
   Gao, Ver Steeg, and Galstyan emphasize that estimating high-dimensional MI is difficult, so practical methods often replace it with low-order approximations based on restrictive and mutually inconsistent assumptions [237] [242]. Their VMI method instead treats the true MI as the target and constructs a tractable variational lower bound, \(I(x:y)\ge I_{\mathrm{LB}}(x:y)\), using an auxiliary distribution \(q\) [221] [250]. Feature selection then maximizes this lower bound rather than estimating the full MI directly [169] [184]. In this paper, MI is therefore an ideal quantity whose approximation is the central methodological problem.

   A related global-feature-selection paper makes the same distinction from a computational perspective: selecting a subset with maximum MI is motivated theoretically, but estimating the joint distribution for a feature subset is often intractable [289] [298]. It therefore assumes conditional independence so that subset MI can be approximated using pairwise conditional mutual-information terms, yielding an NP-hard binary quadratic problem that is then solved approximately [314] [317] [326].

3. **MI as one option among competing dependence measures.**  
   Senawi, Wei, and Billings explicitly develop MRmMC partly to avoid an MI-based criterion. They note that MI can measure arbitrary dependence and apply to discrete as well as numerical variables, but that continuous-variable MI requires density estimation and different estimators introduce tuning parameters and possible estimation error [1499] [1527] [1547]. Their alternative uses conditional-variance correlation for relevance and squared multiple correlation for redundancy [1478] [1504]. MI is consequently treated not as the unavoidable objective, but as one possible design choice that can be replaced by correlation-based alternatives; the paper evaluates MRmMC against MI-based mRMR and MIFS [1464] [1495].

Overall, MI moves from being the **objective to maximize**, to being an **intractable population quantity approximated by bounds or structural assumptions**, and finally to being **one candidate dependence measure whose advantages and estimation costs are weighed against alternatives**.
question_answers.global-train-018:
“Redundancy” is not a single standardized statistic. Different feature-selection papers operationalize it as pairwise information, dependence, correlation, temporal similarity, or predictability from the already selected features.

1. **Pairwise mutual information — Ding and Peng’s mRMR.**  
   In the original mRMR formulation, redundancy is the average mutual information between pairs of selected features:
   \[
   R(S)=\frac{1}{|S|^2}\sum_{i,j\in S} I(i,j).
   \]
   Thus, two features are redundant when knowing one provides substantial information about the other. The paper combines this redundancy term with feature–class relevance using either a difference criterion (MID) or a quotient criterion (MIQ). [1166] [1188] [1213]  
   For continuous variables, the same paper instead proposes correlation-based alternatives: redundancy can be the average absolute Pearson correlation, with FCD using a difference and FCQ using a quotient. [1169] [1182] [1221]

2. **Kernel dependence via HSIC — HSIC Lasso and N3LARS.**  
   Yamada et al.’s HSIC-based methods compute redundancy from the dependence between kernel Gram matrices for two features. In HSIC Lasso, the pairwise redundancy term is
   \[
   \operatorname{HSIC}(u_k,u_l)
   =\operatorname{tr}(\bar K^{(k)}\bar K^{(l)}),
   \]
   where the Gram matrices are centered and normalized. [87]  
   N3LARS uses the normalized version, NHSIC, in an analogous quadratic penalty:
   \[
   \sum_{k,l}\alpha_k\alpha_l\,\operatorname{NHSIC}(u_k,u_l).
   \]
   Highly dependent features therefore receive a large penalty, encouraging one of them to be excluded. [81] [111]

3. **Nonlinear dependence through RDC — the Uber mRMR extensions.**  
   Zhao et al. replace ordinary correlation with the Randomized Dependence Coefficient (RDC) when redundancy may be nonlinear. RDC first applies empirical copula/rank transformations, maps each variable through random nonlinear projections, and computes the largest canonical correlation between the projected representations. [425]  
   The resulting redundancy is the average pairwise RDC between a candidate feature and the already selected features. In the paper’s FRQ variant, for example,
   \[
   f_{\mathrm{FRQ}}(X_i)
   =
   \frac{F(Y,X_i)}
   {\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{X_s\in S}\rho_{\mathrm{rdc}}(X_s,X_i)}.
   \]
   Thus, nonlinear—not merely linear—association is treated as redundancy. [403] [441]

4. **Temporal similarity using dynamic time warping — Radovic et al.’s TMRMR.**  
   For multivariate temporal gene-expression data, Radovic et al. do not flatten each time series and use ordinary correlation. They compute a DTW distance matrix between the temporal profiles of two genes. [873]  
   They then define two redundancy measures: \(R_c\) averages DTW distances over every pair of observations/rows, whereas \(R_m\) uses only distances between corresponding rows. [944] The method therefore treats similarity of temporal trajectories—including curves that are out of phase—as the relevant notion of redundancy. [923]

5. **Multicollinearity/predictability from the selected set — Senawi, Wei, and Billings’ MRmMC.**  
   MRmMC defines redundancy as how well a candidate feature can be predicted from the already selected features. It orthogonalizes the selected features and computes a squared multiple-correlation coefficient; high \(R^2\) means that much of the candidate’s variation is explained by the selected set and is therefore redundant. [1440] [1502]  
   The selection criterion subtracts this multicollinearity measure from a relevance score, rather than subtracting pairwise mutual information. [1467] [1504]

6. **Simple empirical correlation-rate summaries — N3LARS evaluation.**  
   A related but simpler operationalization appears in the N3LARS experiments: redundancy is reported as the mean absolute Pearson correlation among selected features,
   \[
   \mathrm{RED}
   =
   \frac{1}{m(m-1)}
   \sum_{k>l}|\rho_{k,l}|.
   \]
   This is an evaluation statistic for how correlated the selected features are, rather than the nonlinear selection penalty used by N3LARS itself. [154]

Overall, the papers differ in what “duplicate information” means: pairwise mutual information, kernel dependence, nonlinear copula dependence, similarity of temporal trajectories, or the ability to reconstruct one feature from the others. Consequently, two methods can assign different redundancy values—and select different feature subsets—even on the same data. [1166] [87] [425] [944] [1502]
question_answers.global-train-019:
Across the collection, “relevance” is not a single concept. It is variously treated as statistical dependence, class-separation power, nonlinear association, or even model-specific predictive usefulness. The main differences are as follows.

1. **Mutual information in classical mRMR (Ding and Peng).**  
   Ding and Peng measure the relevance of a feature \(g_i\) to the class variable \(h\) by mutual information, \(I(h,g_i)\), and define the relevance of a selected set as the average feature–class mutual information [1188][1202]. Mutual information is appropriate because it detects general dependence rather than only linear association, and it can be used for categorical variables through the joint probability distribution [1264]. The paper uses this measure particularly for discrete gene-expression variables, where strong differential expression across classes should produce large mutual information [1264]. Relevance is then combined with mutual-information redundancy between features, because selecting only highly class-associated genes can produce many correlated and therefore wasteful features [1179][1226]. For continuous data, the paper instead uses the **F-statistic** as the relevance measure, since it directly measures between-class variation relative to within-class variation [1209][1171]. Thus, the choice depends partly on data type: MI for categorical variables and F-statistics for continuous variables [1171].

2. **F-statistic averaged across time in temporal mRMR (Radovic et al.).**  
   For multivariate temporal gene-expression data, Radovic et al. define a gene’s relevance by calculating an F-statistic separately at each time point and then taking the arithmetic mean across time [862][884]. This was chosen because flattening a temporal profile into a single vector can lose temporal structure and can even make opposing temporal trends appear weakly relevant [869][908]. The arithmetic mean was preferred over median, geometric mean, or maximum: median and geometric mean may miss genes whose class differences occur only during a short period, whereas the maximum ignores the rest of the trajectory; the mean retains evidence distributed across time while still producing a single relevance score [875][900][906]. In this paper, relevance therefore means persistent or aggregate class separation across the temporal record, rather than dependence with a class label after discarding time.

3. **Randomized nonlinear dependence in RDC (Lopez-Paz, Hennig, and Schölkopf).**  
   The Randomized Dependence Coefficient measures relevance as a nonlinear dependence score: the largest canonical correlation between randomly chosen nonlinear projections of the empirical copula transformations of the feature and target [44][46][52]. This was chosen because Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall measures cover only limited association patterns, such as linear or monotonic relationships [15][26]. RDC is intended to capture nonlinear dependence, to work with variables of arbitrary dimension, and to remain invariant to monotonic transformations of marginal distributions [48][58]. The copula transformation removes the individual marginal forms while preserving the dependence structure [2][17], making the score focus on the relationship itself rather than on shifts or rescalings of feature values. Random nonlinear projections make the HGR-style idea computationally feasible: the exact HGR coefficient is an infinite-dimensional, computationally intractable supremum [25], whereas RDC provides a finite-dimensional approximation with approximately \(O(n\log n)\) sample complexity [57].

4. **Normalized HSIC in N3LARS (Yamada et al.).**  
   N3LARS uses the normalized Hilbert–Schmidt Independence Criterion (NHSIC) as the feature–target relevance score [84][93]. The relevance of feature \(u_k\) is \(NHSIC(u_k,y)\); a large score increases the feature’s coefficient, while a score near zero indicates independence and makes the feature less likely to be selected [95][106]. This measure was chosen to capture nonlinear dependence in a model-independent filter method, unlike ordinary Lasso, which can capture only linear dependence [157][163]. A universal Gaussian kernel is used because HSIC with such a kernel is zero if and only if the variables are statistically independent [72][87]. NHSIC is also convenient for the proposed optimization: it can be written through centered Gram matrices and integrated into a non-negative LARS objective that simultaneously rewards feature–target dependence and penalizes feature–feature dependence [81][97].

5. **Conditional-variance correlation in MRmMC (Senawi, Wei, and Billings).**  
   The MRmMC paper uses a correlation measure based on conditional variance to quantify feature relevance to a nominal class. The measure lies between zero and one: values near one indicate strong dependence, while zero indicates independence or lack of correlation [1512][1548]. It is motivated by the need to handle quantitative features and nominal class labels directly, where common correlation measures are often restricted to particular data-type combinations [1538][1554]. The authors also avoid mutual information because estimating MI for continuous variables requires estimating an unknown density and often involves tuning parameters or approximations [1527][1547]. Thus, MRmMC chooses conditional-variance correlation for a comparatively simple, parameter-free relevance score that is comparable with its redundancy measure [1450][1563].

6. **F-statistic or model-based relevance in marketing mRMR variants (Zhao et al.).**  
   The marketing-platform paper deliberately varies the relevance measure according to the intended use. Its baseline MID and MIQ methods use mutual information between feature and response, but FCD and FCQ replace MI with the F-statistic [400][391]. The F-statistic was selected as a faster alternative for continuous variables; however, the paper notes that a difference between F-statistic relevance and correlation-based redundancy can be poorly scaled, because the F-statistic is unbounded whereas correlation lies between zero and one [403][456]. The authors therefore use a quotient form, FCQ, to reduce the effect of scale imbalance [453]. They also introduce model-based relevance, using Random Forest feature-importance scores in RFCQ and RFRQ, because relevance can be made specific to a known downstream model [404][441]. This is chosen when the production classifier is known in advance, whereas FCQ is retained as a model-free option with broader applicability across classifiers [445][491].

Overall, the collection spans a continuum: **MI** measures general information shared with the class; **F-statistics** measure class separation, often efficiently for continuous data; **RDC** and **HSIC** measure broad nonlinear dependence; **temporal F-statistics** preserve relevance distributed across time; **conditional-variance correlation** avoids difficult density estimation; and **Random Forest importance** measures relevance in the sense of usefulness to a particular predictive model. The different choices reflect differences in data type, temporal structure, nonlinear versus linear dependence, computational constraints, and whether relevance is intended to be model-independent or tied to a downstream classifier.
